paper.title: No Time Like the Present: Agentic Test-Time Training for LLM Agents

reader_profile.language: English and Simplified Chinese, equivalent paired blocks

claims.claim:
### Key concepts: why adapting during action is different
An LLM agent alternates between observing an environment and producing reasoning plus an action. Test-time training (TTT) changes model parameters during inference. In a static task, the adaptation input is given; in an interactive task, the current policy helps create the next observation and the text on which it will train. A failed action can therefore return the same observation, prompt another similar action, and supply another training example reinforcing the loop. This **endogenous data distribution** is the paper’s central problem, not merely an insufficient context window.

claims.claim: The proposed aTTT uses low-rank adaptation (LoRA), which means a small trainable parameter update alongside frozen base weights. Each episode owns its adapter and repetition history; both reset for the next task. It is unsupervised next-token learning, not reward-based reinforcement learning, cross-task lifelong memory, or a verified correction of the agent’s beliefs. The key hypothesis is that novel pieces of the current trajectory are more useful adaptation data than repeated fragments. Novelty is a proxy, not a correctness label.

claims.claim: Key observation and interpretation. Figure 2 shows a trajectory buffer feeding one of three text sources every K interaction steps; repetition-aware weights then shape a gradient update before the agent continues. Self uses the latest agent message, including reasoning and action; Env uses the latest observation; Summary asks another LLM call to summarize the trajectory. Self and Env cannot retrain on the entire prefix. This supports an online feedback-loop interpretation: parameters influence subsequent observations. The diagram cannot establish that any source is truthful, or that a gradient step is beneficial.

claims.claim: Let τₜ be the observation/message history and xₖ the selected update text. Equations 1–2 use ordinary next-token negative log likelihood: each token is predicted from its preceding tokens, and θ moves against the loss gradient with learning rate η. No success label is required. This is also the danger: maximizing likelihood of a repeated bad plan can make that plan easier to produce.

claims.claim: Key observation and interpretation. The horizontal axis counts updates and the vertical axis measures update-text repetition. On Qwen3.5-9B with Self, failed episodes rise earlier and remain more repetitive than successful ones. This supports testing repetition-aware learning, but the observational comparison cannot establish that repetition caused failure: difficult tasks can cause both. The diagnostic uses maximum word-set Jaccard overlap with a previous update, ρ(xₖ)=max |W(xₖ)∩W(x′)|/|W(xₖ)∪W(x′)|; novelty is 1−ρ, with zero repetition on the first update. Word sets ignore order and multiplicity. A sequence-level baseline skips updates below novelty 0.5; that is distinct from aTTT’s token weighting.

claims.claim:
### Token weights: preserving new information inside repeated text
For each current token j, enumerate the n-grams containing it and find their largest occurrence count in **previous** tokenized update texts. That maximum is fₖ(j). Give the token weight max(wₘᵢₙ,1/(1+fₖ(j))). A previously unseen local pattern has weight 1; count 1 gives 1/2; count 3 gives 1/4; the floor 0.05 avoids deleting the learning signal entirely. Taking the maximum makes a token conservative if any enclosing n-gram is familiar. The actual objective divides by token count L, not by the sum of weights: it changes both where the gradient points and its effective magnitude.

claims.claim: Key observation and interpretation. Algorithm 1 orders tokenization, historical counts, weighting, gradient descent and history append. The final append matters: counting the current example as past exposure would wrongly suppress its first appearance. As a worked example, suppose a repeated “look at shelf” fragment has count 3 while a new location fragment has count 0. Their token weights become 0.25 and 1, respectively; the update still uses the whole sequence but learns four times more strongly from the latter at equal token loss. This supports selective adaptation within a mixed observation; it cannot make an unfamiliar false statement safe to learn. Default settings are n=3, K=5, LoRA rank 8/α16, learning rate 5×10⁻⁴ and two gradient steps per update.

claims.claim: Key observation and interpretation. Figure 9’s left panel groups action changes by the base model’s action margin: low-margin decisions change most, while high-margin decisions rarely flip. Its right panel shows increased cross-seed action diversity. This supports a local decision-perturbation account, not calibrated uncertainty estimation. Figure 10 supplies the end-to-end example: both agents explore identically through step 8 in a two-soapbars-to-garbagecan task. At step 9 the baseline puts its soapbar back and loops until step 50; aTTT delivers the first soapbar, returns for the second and finishes at step 14. The capacity constraint makes “try to pick up another item while holding one” unproductive; changing that decision unlocks the rest of the plan. This is an illustrative selected rescue, not evidence that all failures share this cause or that every update helps.

claims.claim:
### Evaluation contract
ALFWorld contains 140 tasks: 103 pick-and-place, 24 pick-two and 13 look-at-object tasks, capped at 50 interaction steps. SWE-bench Lite uses 150 instances with mini-swe-agent and a 150-call cap, not the entire 300-instance Lite benchmark. Tables report mean ± standard error across three seeds. Small subgroups and three seeds limit precision; percentages should not be read as universal expected gains.

claims.claim:
Key observation and interpretation. Table 1 shows Qwen3.5-9B rising from 50.7±0.8 to 55.7±1.4 with Self+aTTT, a 5.0 percentage-point gain; Env+aTTT is 55.5±1.3 and Summary+aTTT 54.3±0.7. Gemma-3-12B rises from 22.4±0.6 to 26.7±0.6 with Summary. The strongest token-weighted 4B result is Summary 4.8±0.2 versus baseline 1.9±0.5. Table 2 shows SWE-bench 27B improving 57.8±0.6→62.7±1.0, and 9B 35.6±0.4→38.4±0.6. This supports useful online adaptation where the model has some competence and enough trajectory remains. Boundary: Figure 4 is a cross-regime synthesis, not a controlled proof that model size or horizon causes the gain.

**Source reconciliation:** Figure 4/Table 3 advertise a 4B +3.6 gain, which corresponds to Table 1’s Env **sequence-filter** score 5.5, not token-weighted aTTT’s best 4.8 (+2.9). Table 2 labels the 9B gain +2.9 although its displayed endpoints subtract to +2.8, plausibly rounding. Keep the original endpoints and variant names rather than silently merging these claims.

claims.claim: Key observation and interpretation. Figure 5 breaks success down by task family; the pick-two setting offers the clearest gain, consistent with needing sustained progress across multiple searches. Figure 6 compares adapter/base-model KL divergence on failed episodes and repetition on matched rescued pairs. Unfiltered learning drifts farther from the base policy; aTTT keeps the divergence smaller. In rescued pairs, baseline repetition rises later while aTTT finishes earlier (mean 26.3 steps versus the 50-step limit). This supports the proposed failure-loop mechanism, but the subset is selected using outcomes: it cannot estimate the population rescue probability or prove that smaller KL alone causes success. The 13-task look-at-object group is especially small.

claims.claim: Key observation and interpretation. Table 3 shows different failure profiles: 4B has 30% invalid actions, versus 2% for 9B and 6% for Gemma-12B; immediate repeats are 71%, 31% and 7%. The best signal therefore varies, but selecting it after a sweep is descriptive, not a predictor validated on held-out models. Figure 7 matches the repetition filter’s update-drop rate with random dropping; random removal cannot match the gain. This supports **which data are retained** over “just train less,” but cannot fully separate token-content weighting from reduced gradient magnitude. Table 4 varies K on 9B Self: K=1/2/5/10 gives 51.0/51.9/55.7/54.5%, with novelty 0.42/0.42/0.56/0.58. More frequent updates are not better; fresh evidence must accumulate. The error bars and limited sweep cannot establish a universal optimal cadence.

claims.claim: Key observation and interpretation. Figure 8 separates frozen-base inference from training engines, maintains private per-episode LoRA adapters, and hot-swaps updates into vLLM while other episodes continue. The implementation runs 16 concurrent episodes and reports sub-100-ms adapter swaps. Table 5 measures 140 ALFWorld episodes: no-TTT 14.6 minutes, concurrent aTTT 28.3, sequential TTT 186.0. This supports practical latency reduction through concurrency: 1.9× baseline time rather than a sequential bottleneck, and 6.6× faster than that sequential implementation. It cannot show equal GPU-hours, energy, or dollar cost; separate training resources are used.

claims.claim: Key observation and interpretation. Table 6 reports rank sensitivity on Qwen3.5-27B: relative to rank 8, ranks 4/16/32 change success by −0.7/−1.4/−4.3 points. Table 7 tests Summary on 9B: n=2/3/4/5 gives 52.8±1.8/54.3±0.7/54.5±0.6/54.1±0.8. This supports a reasonably broad local choice around rank 8 and n=3–5; they cannot establish robustness to arbitrary optimizers or environments. Appendix E also reports context-only summaries at 49.3 and decoding repetition penalty 1.1 at 49.7, below the main-table 50.7 baseline. Its prose mentions 51.4 as a baseline elsewhere, so these controls should be treated as directional comparisons rather than silently harmonized exact deltas.
